structure.title: exit-site infections: signs and prevention
structure.summary: An exit-site infection occurs where the catheter leaves your skin. If left untreated, it can travel inward and cause peritonitis.
structure.text:
An exit-site infection occurs where the catheter leaves your skin. If left untreated, it can travel inward and cause peritonitis.

### Signs and Symptoms:
- **Redness, swelling, warmth, or tenderness** around the site.
- **Pus or discharge:** Yellow, green, or cloudy fluid.
- **Pain:** Soreness when touching the area.

### 10 Rules for Prevention:
1. **No Tugging:** Avoid trauma or pulling the catheter.
2. **Hand Hygiene:** Wash hands or use alcohol rub before touching the site.
3. **Dryness:** Never use wet dressing sets or gauze.
4. **Daily Check:** Inspect the exit site every single day.
5. **No Ad-hoc Creams:** Do not use powders or ointments unless prescribed.
6. **No Scissors:** Never use scissors near your catheter.
7. **Clean Skin:** Use antibacterial soap while bathing.
8. **Anchoring:** Always tape in a **"C" shape** to prevent movement.
9. **Loose Clothing:** Avoid tight belts or waistbands over the site.
10. **Safe Bathing:** Never submerge in pools, tubs, or rivers.

### What to Do if Symptoms Appear:
- **Contact your doctor immediately.** They may take a culture test of any pus. You will likely be prescribed antibiotics.

structure.title: troubleshooting slow flow and fibrin
structure.summary: Most flow issues during an exchange are easy to solve.
structure.text:
Most flow issues during an exchange are easy to solve.

### Problem: Slow Drainage or Fill 🐢
1. **Check Tubing:** Look for kinks or twists and straighten them.
2. **Check Clamps:** Ensure all required clamps are fully open.
3. **Check Position:** New bag must be high; drain bag must be on the floor. **Gravity is your friend.**
4. **Check for Fibrin:** If you see white, stringy bits (fibrin) blocking the flow, gently squeeze the tubing. Tell your nurse if you see this often.
5. **Change Position:** Stand up, sit down, or roll to your side to shift the catheter tip.
6. **Constipation:** A full bowel can block flow. Talk to your team about stool softeners.

structure.title: troubleshooting leaks and hernias
structure.summary: Peritoneal boundary defects can cause fluid to escape or tissues to bulge.
structure.text:
Peritoneal boundary defects can cause fluid to escape or tissues to bulge.

### Pericatheter Leaks 💧
- **Early Leaks:** Often from starting dialysis too soon before the skin has healed.
- **Late Leaks:** Usually from physical strain or an underlying hernia.
- **What to do:** Clamp your catheter, drain any fluid inside you, cover the site with dry sterile gauze, and **call your clinic immediately**.

### Hernias
Bulges at the belly button, groin, or catheter site can appear due to the pressure of the fluid. These require surgical repair. Report any new bulges to your team.

structure.title: managing pain and other pd complications
structure.summary: While PD is generally comfortable, you may occasionally experience these complications:
structure.text:
While PD is generally comfortable, you may occasionally experience these complications:

### Pain During Exchange
- **Inflow Pain:** Pain as fluid enters. Ensure the solution is warm and try slowing the fill rate.
- **Outflow (Drain) Pain:** Sharp "siphon pain" at the very end of the drain. Your nurse can adjust your cycler, or you can clamp the line just before the drain is totally complete.

### Fluid Appearance Issues
- **Bloody Fluid (Hemoperitoneum):** Drain fluid appears pink or red. In women, this is often due to ovulation/menstruation. Report it to your clinic; usually, it resolves on its own.
- **Air in Abdomen (Pneumoperitoneum):** Can cause shoulder pain. Usually occurs if air isn't properly flushed from tubing before an exchange.

### Urgent Contamination ⚠️
- **Tubing Disconnect/Break:** Immediately **CLAMP** close to your body. Cover with a sterile cap or gauze and call your clinic immediately.
- **Touch Contamination:** If you touch a sterile part (end of tubing/inside of cap), throw it away and start over with a new set.

structure.title: a guide to common concerns on pd: when to call your clinic
structure.summary: As you adjust to life on PD, you will become an expert in your body. Use this guide to identify issues and know when to seek help.
structure.text:
As you adjust to life on PD, you will become an expert in your body. Use this guide to identify issues and know when to seek help.

### What Your Drain Bag is Telling You
The appearance of your drained fluid is a vital clue to your health.
- **The Newspaper Test:** After each exchange, hold the drain bag against a piece of paper with writing on it. If you cannot read the text through the fluid, it is **cloudy**—this is a sign of peritonitis. Call your clinic immediately.

### Understanding Aches and Pains
- **Abdominal (Belly) Pain:** Constant, dull, or sharp pain is NOT normal. If your belly hurts and the fluid is cloudy, it is peritonitis.
- **Shoulder Tip Pain:** Usually caused by trapped air irritating a nerve. Try lying down or using a warm pack. It is generally not dangerous.
- **Chest Pain:** This is an **EMERGENCY**. Call your clinic and go to the nearest hospital immediately.
- **Drain (Siphon) Pain:** Sharp pain at the very end of a drain. Try changing positions or slowing the drain speed. Discuss with your nurse.

### Urgent Symptoms
- **Shortness of Breath:** If you can't catch your breath, especially when lying down, fluid may be building up in your lungs. Call your clinic immediately.
- **Sudden Swelling:** New lumps (hernias) or soft swelling in the abdomen, genitals, or thighs (leaks) must be reported promptly.

structure.title: managing common health issues on pd
structure.summary: Many side effects of kidney disease can be managed with your team:
structure.text:
Many side effects of kidney disease can be managed with your team:

- **Itchy Skin:** Often due to high phosphate. Take your **phosphate binders** with meals, follow your diet, and use unscented moisturizer (away from the exit site).
- **Constipation:** A full bowel can block your catheter flow. Eat high-fibre foods and talk to your doctor about stool softeners.
- **Fatigue (Anemia):** Feeling very tired is common. Your team may prescribe iron or EPO injections to help make red blood cells.
- **Leg Cramps:** Let your nurse know if you experience restless legs or cramps, as your treatment may need adjustment.

structure.title: exercise and swimming on peritoneal dialysis
structure.summary: Staying active is a vital part of health on PD, offering both physical and mental benefits.
structure.text:
Staying active is a vital part of health on PD, offering both physical and mental benefits.

### Benefits of Exercise
- Increases energy and fights fatigue.
- Helps control weight and improves sleep/stress.
- Strengthens muscles and maintains independence.

### Recommended Activities
- **Outdoor:** Brisk walking, jogging, cycling.
- **Indoor:** Treadmill, dancing, light weights.
- **⚠️ Important:** Avoid heavy lifting and exercises that strain the abdomen (like sit-ups) to prevent hernias. Do not exercise when your belly is full of fluid.

### A Warning About Swimming 🏊
Your team strongly advises **against** swimming in pools, lakes, rivers, or hot tubs due to the high risk of infection. 
- If you choose to swim in a private, well-maintained pool, you **must** use a waterproof dressing and perform complete exit-site care immediately after.

structure.title: storing and disposing of pd supplies
structure.summary: Proper storage and disposal maintain safety and hygiene at home.
structure.text:
Proper storage and disposal maintain safety and hygiene at home.

### Storing Your Supplies
- **DO:** Keep in original unopened cases at room temperature. Use the "oldest first" (FIFO) rule.
- **DON'T:** Store in direct sunlight, damp areas (attics/sheds), near heat sources (radiators/stoves), or next to chemicals/pesticides.
- **Space:** Your storage area should be clear, reachable, and at least 5 feet high by 7 feet wide.

### Disposing of Waste
- **Used Fluid:** Empty all fluids into a toilet or clean drain. If using a cycler, an oversized drain bag on a cart makes transport easier.
- **Cleaning Drains:** Clean waste drains weekly by pouring a mild bleach solution (1/4 cup bleach to 1 quart water) down while running hot water.
- **Supplies:** Most items go in a sealed plastic bag in regular household trash. **Do not recycle** dialysis tubing or bags.
- **⚠️ Sharps:** Never throw needles in regular trash; use your provided puncture-proof sharps container.

structure.title: medications on peritoneal dialysis
structure.summary: Your medications are a vital part of your treatment, working together with dialysis and diet to keep you healthy.
structure.text:
Your medications are a vital part of your treatment, working together with dialysis and diet to keep you healthy.

### 4 Golden Rules for Medication Safety:
1. **Always Ask:** Never take ANY new medicine (OTC, herbal, or from another doctor) without talking to your PD team first.
2. **Know Allergies:** Remind your team of any allergies every time they prescribe something new.
3. **Understand Your Meds:** Know the name, dose, timing, and why you are taking each medicine.
4. **Bring Your Meds:** Bring all original bottles or strips to every clinic visit for review.

### Common PD Medications:
- **Phosphate Binders:** **CRITICAL:** Take **WITH** meals/snacks. They "bind" phosphate in food so your body doesn't absorb it.
- **Active Vitamin D:** Helps your body absorb calcium to keep bones strong.
- **Iron:** Builds red blood cells to fight anemia and tiredness. Tablets work best on an empty stomach (but can be taken with food if they upset it).
- **Kidney-Specific Multivitamins:** Replaces vitamins washed out during dialysis. Do not take standard OTC multivitamins.
- **Stool Softeners/Laxatives:** Prevents constipation, which can block your catheter or cause pain.
- **EPO Injections:** A hormone injection that tells your body to make red blood cells, boosting energy levels.

### ⚠️ Pain Relief Safety Alert:
- **SAFE:** Paracetamol (Crocin, Calpol) is usually the safest choice.
- **AVOID:** NSAIDs (Ibuprofen/Brufen, Diclofenac/Voveran, Combiflam) can harm your remaining kidney function.

### Special Situation Meds:
- **Heparin:** Used to prevent catheter blockage if you see white stringy bits (fibrin) in your fluid.
- **Antibiotics:** Used for exit-site or belly infections. **Finish the full course** even if you feel better.
- **Pre-Procedure:** Always tell your PD team before ANY procedure (dental, minor surgery) as you may need preventive antibiotics.

structure.title: pd for different health situations
structure.summary: PD is a flexible therapy that works well for many patients with diverse health backgrounds.
structure.text:
PD is a flexible therapy that works well for many patients with diverse health backgrounds.

- **Diabetes:** PD is a safe and effective choice for patients with diabetes.
- **Older Adults:** Age is not a barrier; PD is a great option for many elderly patients.
- **Obesity:** Being overweight does not prevent successful outcomes on PD.
- **Urgent Start:** If you need to start unexpectedly, 'Urgent Start PD' can often avoid the need for a temporary hemodialysis catheter.
- **ADPKD:** Even with very large kidneys, PD is a safe and effective choice.
- **Prior Surgery:** Most prior abdominal surgeries (like C-sections or gallbladder removal) do not prevent successful PD.
- **LVAD (Heart Pump):** PD is often preferred as it is gentler on blood pressure.
- **Stoma/Colostomy:** Possible with a 'presternal' catheter placed on the upper chest, away from the stoma.

structure.title: essential vaccinations for pd patients
structure.summary: Because PD can weaken your immune system, staying up-to-date on vaccinations is your best shield against serious illness.
structure.text:
Because PD can weaken your immune system, staying up-to-date on vaccinations is your best shield against serious illness.

### Key Vaccinations:
- **Hepatitis B:** A series of shots to protect your liver. Your team will check your immunity first.
- **Pneumococcal (Pneumonia):** Usually a single shot to protect your lungs; a booster may be needed after 5 years.
- **Flu & COVID-19:** Annual flu shots (May-June in India) and current COVID boosters are critical for preventing severe respiratory complications.
- **Tetanus:** A booster shot is needed every 10 years to protect against 'lockjaw' from cuts/wounds.
- **Travel Vaccines:** If traveling (locally or abroad), speak to your team 4–6 weeks ahead to check if you need Typhoid or Hepatitis A vaccines.

structure.title: adding medications to your pd bags (intraperitoneal)
structure.summary: Many medications (like antibiotics or insulin) are added directly into the dialysis bag. Proper technique is critical to prevent infection.
structure.text:
Many medications (like antibiotics or insulin) are added directly into the dialysis bag. Proper technique is critical to prevent infection.

### Materials Required:
- Syringe and Needle
- Gauze & Sterile Bowl
- Sterile Napkin
- Povidone Iodine
- Medication vial

### Step-by-Step Procedure:
1. **Mask & Initial Wash:** Put on your mask and perform a simple hand wash.
2. **Setup:** Place a sterile sheet on a clean table. Open supplies (gauze, syringe, needle) onto it. Pour Iodine into the bowl.
3. **Meticulous Wash:** Perform the **full six-step hand wash** and dry with a sterile napkin.
4. **Clean Ports:** Wrap Iodine-soaked gauze around the **medication port** on the bag. Clean the top of the medication vial with a separate soaked gauze.
5. **Draw Med:** Use the syringe to draw the prescribed amount.
6. **New Needle:** **Change the needle** on the syringe before injecting.
7. **Inject:** Carefully insert the new needle into the **center** of the rubber medication port and inject.

### Precautions:
- **Never touch the needle.**
- Insert in the **center** of the port to avoid puncturing the side of the bag.
- Use a **separate sterile syringe and needle** for each different medication.

structure.title: your guide to a kidney-friendly diet on pd
structure.summary: Your diet is a partnership with your dialysis to manage waste and fluid balance.
structure.text:
Your diet is a partnership with your dialysis to manage waste and fluid balance.

### Protein: Increased Needs
PD removes protein along with waste, so you need more of it.
- **Eat:** Fresh chicken, fish, beans, beef, eggs, and tofu.
- **Limit:** Cured and processed deli meats (often high in salt).

### Sodium: Under 2,000 mg/day
Controlling salt prevents high blood pressure, swelling, and shortness of breath.
- **Eat:** Home-cooked meals seasoned with herbs and spices.
- **Avoid:** Packaged/processed foods, canned goods, frozen dinners, and fast food.

### Phosphorus: 800–1,000 mg/day
Prevents bone and heart damage.
- **Avoid:** Dairy (milk, yogurt, cheese), processed meats, chocolate, nuts, and flavored drinks.
- **Phosphate Binders:** Take these **with every meal** as prescribed.

### Potassium & Calories
- **Potassium:** PD is efficient at removing potassium, so you may have more flexibility (3,000–4,000 mg/day).
- **Calories:** Your dialysis fluid contains sugar (dextrose), giving you extra calories. You may need to eat fewer calorie-rich carbs to maintain a healthy weight.

### Fibre & Calcium
- **Fibre (20–25g):** Helps control blood sugar and prevents constipation.
- **Calcium (Under 2,000mg):** Total intake from food and medicine should be restricted to prevent "vascular calcification."

### Fluid Balance
Stick to about **4 cups (1 Litre)** of fluid per day, including soups and water-rich fruits like watermelon. Minimizing salt is the best way to control thirst.

structure.title: low-sodium (low-salt) diet for peritoneal dialysis
structure.summary: Cutting back on sodium is one of the most important things you can do for your health on PD. It helps control blood pressure and prevents fluid overlo
structure.text:
Cutting back on sodium is one of the most important things you can do for your health on PD. It helps control blood pressure and prevents fluid overload/swelling.

### Where is Sodium Hiding?
Most sodium comes from processed and restaurant foods:
- **Canned/Pickled:** Canned foods, **pickles (achar)**, and **papad**.
- **Snacks:** **Bhujia**, chips, salted nuts.
- **Processed:** Cheese, sauces, chutneys, instant soup, breads.

### 5 Tips for Cutting Sodium:
1. **Cook at Home:** Full control over salt usage.
2. **Read Labels:** Look for "Low Sodium" or "No Salt Added".
3. **No Table Salt:** Remove the salt shaker. Taste food before adding any.
4. **Flavor with Herbs:** Use lemon juice, **amchur** (mango powder), garlic, onion, or ginger.
5. **Rinse:** If using canned beans/veg, rinse them under water.

### Foods to Choose (Lower Sodium):
- **Vegetables:** Fresh **lauki, tori, tinda, bhindi**.
- **Grains:** Roti or chapati made **without salt** in the dough; unpolished rice; scratch-cooked dals.
- **Dairy:** Homemade **dahi** (yogurt) and **paneer** (unsalted).

### Foods to Avoid (Higher Sodium):
- **Achar** (all kinds) and **Papad**.
- **Bhujia**, salted peanuts, soy sauce.
- **Salty Additions:** Bouillon cubes, baking soda, and **chaat masala** in large quantities.

structure.title: low-potassium diet for peritoneal dialysis
structure.summary: Potassium keeps your heart beating regularly, but too much (**hyperkalemia**) is dangerous. PD is efficient at removing it, but many still need to be
structure.text:
Potassium keeps your heart beating regularly, but too much (**hyperkalemia**) is dangerous. PD is efficient at removing it, but many still need to be mindful.

### Foods HIGHER in Potassium (Limit):
- **Fruits:** Mango, banana, orange, pomegranate (**anar**), papaya, **coconut water**, and fruit juices.
- **Vegetables:** Potato, sweet potato (**shakarkandi**), spinach (**palak**), tomatoes, pumpkin (**kaddu**), mushrooms.
- **Other:** Lentils/dals (in large amounts), nuts, milk, yogurt.

### Foods LOWER in Potassium (Better Choices):
- **Fruits:** Apple, pear (**nashpati**), guava (**amrood**), pineapple, berries.
- **Vegetables:** Cabbage (**patta gobhi**), cauliflower (**phool gobhi**), onion, capsicum (**Shimla mirch**), **lauki**, cucumber, radish (**mooli**), brinjal.
- **Grains/Protein:** Rice, wheat (roti), chicken, fish, eggs.

### How to Reduce Potassium (Leaching Process):
You can remove some potassium from potatoes or dals before cooking:
1. **Peel & Cut:** Cut into small, thin pieces.
2. **Rinse:** Rinse under warm water.
3. **Soak:** Soak in warm, unsalted water for **at least 2 hours** (10 parts water to 1 part veg).
4. **Drain & Rinse:** Throw away soaking water and rinse again.
5. **Cook:** Boil in fresh, unsalted water. **Discard the cooking water.**
